prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: Doubt at the Consecration
In 1411, a priest was celebrating Mass in the chapel of Count Batthyany's castle at Ludbreg, in what is now northern Croatia.
At the consecration of the wine, he found himself gripped by sudden doubt over the truth of transubstantiation—whether the wine in the chalice before him truly became the Blood of Christ.
At that very moment, tradition holds, the wine turned visibly into Blood.
Hidden in the Wall

Rather than report what had happened, the priest, uncertain how to proceed and perhaps fearful of the consequences, had a workman seal the chalice and its contents into the wall behind the main altar, swearing the man to secrecy.
The priest himself told no one, and only revealed what he had hidden on his deathbed, years later.
Recovered and Sent to Rome
The chalice was retrieved from the wall exactly as it had been left, its contents still intact.
Word of the relic eventually reached the Holy See, which had it brought to Rome for a period of examination.
Pope Leo X issued a bull in 1513 permitting its veneration, after which the relic was returned to Ludbreg and placed in the parish Church of the Holy Trinity, where it has remained ever since.
A Reliquary and a Vow
In 1721, Countess Eleonora Batthyany-Strattman donated a gold and jewel-set reliquary, crafted by the Augsburg goldsmiths' guild, still used to display the relic today.
In 1739, as plague spread through the region, the Croatian Parliament vowed to build a new chapel at Ludbreg if the epidemic were stopped.
The plague passed, though years of subsequent war delayed construction of the promised chapel until 1993.
It was completed in 1994, after Croatia's own passage to independent, democratic government.
Legacy
Ludbreg marks the anniversary each year in the first week of September with a week-long celebration known locally as Sveta Nedjelja, Holy Sunday, drawing pilgrims from across Croatia and beyond.
Counted by many alongside Lanciano and Santarém among the most significant Eucharistic traditions in the Church's history, Ludbreg's relic carries an unusual double witness.
One is a priest's fear-driven silence lasting a lifetime; the other, a count's family still guarding, three centuries later, the reliquary made to honor what that silence eventually gave way to.
